ethiopia.title: Ethiopian Authorities Suspend Independent Newspaper
ethiopia.content: Ethiopian Authorities Suspend Independent Newspaper - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopian Authorities Suspend Independent Newspaper 3 November 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) By Laetitia Bader Government Should Lift Ban, End Attacks on Media In what has become the new normal, the Ethiopian government has silenced yet another independent media outlet. The Ethiopian Media Authority announced in a November 2 Facebook post that it is indefinitely suspending the print and online license of the Reporter , one of Ethiopia's oldest media institutions. Publishing in English and Amharic, the Reporter is also the country's last privately owned Amharic newspaper. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Stating that the suspension would take effect immediately, the Media Authority accused the Reporter of violating the country's laws and media ethics by repeatedly publishing content that was against "national interests." The authority added that the outlet published "distorted content that negatively affects foreign investment, tourism, and diplomacy." The action is part of the government's ongoing assault on the media and civic space in the country and points toward increasing use of vague claims about " national interests " to shut down any critical reporting. Since 2025 , Ethiopian authorities have banned numerous media outlets , deported foreign correspondents , and targeted local journalists through arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, and office raids . In October, undercover police detained journalists Samuel Getachew and Amanuel Gebremedhin, charging them with reporting news that would cause disruptions in Addis Ababa, the capital. The two were jailed for eight days. The Reporter, one of the few remaining independent outlets in the country, hasn't been spared. Authorities have arrested its journalists, while the outlet itself has been under government pressure. Days before the suspension, the Reporter published an editorial warning that Ethiopia's privately owned press was "navigating one of its most precarious periods in history" and calling for immediate reforms to prevent its total collapse. The Ethiopian government should heed the warning; the country's concerned partners should urge the government to immediately reverse course. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian authorities have indefinitely suspended the Reporter, one of the country's oldest independent newspapers, citing violations of national laws and media ethics. The Ethiopian Media Authority announced the suspension on November 2, claiming the outlet published content detrimental to "national interests," which they argued negatively impacts foreign investment, tourism, and diplomacy. This action reflects a broader trend of government repression against media and civil society, with numerous outlets banned and journalists facing arbitrary arrests and intimidation since 2025. The Reporter, which publishes in English and Amharic, is the last privately owned Amharic newspaper in Ethiopia. Prior to its suspension, the outlet warned of a precarious situation for the private press in the country and called for urgent reforms. Human Rights Watch has urged the government to lift the ban and end its attacks on media freedom, emphasizing the need for a more open and democratic environment for journalism in Ethiopia.

ethiopia.title: Kenya Begins Registering Ethiopian Refugees Fleeing Moyale Clashes - Arrivals Surpass 50,000
ethiopia.content: Kenya Begins Registering Ethiopian Refugees Fleeing Moyale Clashes - Arrivals Surpass 50,000 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Kenya Begins Registering Ethiopian Refugees Fleeing Moyale Clashes - Arrivals Surpass 50,000 UNFPA Kenya The ongoing drought and rising insecurity forced Rukia Yaarow Ali to leave her home in Somalia, to seek refuge in Daadab refugee complex in northern Kenya. 3 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Kenyan authorities, in collaboration with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the Kenya Red Cross Society (KRCS), have begun registering Ethiopian refugees fleeing renewed clashes in the border town of Moyale, as more than 50,000 people have reportedly crossed into Kenya since fighting intensified in late October. According to Kenyan media reports the registration exercise began around 31 October at temporary reception sites, including Harhosa and OMC camps in Marsabit County. Registration teams are issuing blue wristbands bearing unique identification codes to document arrivals and establish an initial count of displaced people, including children. The initial registration will be followed by household profiling and the issuance of assistance cards to help identify families, assess their needs and coordinate humanitarian aid, the reports said. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The influx has placed growing pressure on local resources and humanitarian services, with new arrivals continuing to seek safety across the border. Many are sheltering in temporary sites, including schools, churches and camps such as St. Mary's, Manyatta Burji and Sessi, while others are staying with relatives or members of host communities. Humanitarian needs include food, clean water, emergency shelter, sanitation, healthcare and protection services, particularly for women and children. UNHCR, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), UNICEF and other humanitarian partners are coordinating with Kenya's Department of Refugee Services and county authorities. Agencies have appealed for approximately $8.9 million to support the response over three months. The Kenya Red Cross said it has distributed shelter kits, food and other emergency supplies, while Kenyan authorities have heightened security along the border amid reports of stray bullets affecting areas on the Kenyan side. Ethiopia's Moyale, a contested border town jointly administered by the Oromia and Somali regional states, has seen longstanding disputes over territory and administrative authority with some of these disputes in the past leading to recurring tensions between Borana Oromo and Garre Somali communities. The latest escalation followed a dispute over the raising of the Somali Regional State flag and the opening of a related administrative office around 18 October. Tensions intensified following the killing of a 13-year-old girl, identified in local accounts as Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa. By 22 October, clashes had escalated, with reports of heavy gunfire, civilian casualties, injuries and destruction of homes and businesses across Moyale and surrounding areas, including Gumi Eldallo, Wachile and Arero. ethiopia.summary: Kenyan authorities, in collaboration with the UNHCR and the Kenya Red Cross Society, have initiated the registration of over 50,000 Ethiopian refugees fleeing violent clashes in Moyale. The registration began on October 31 at temporary reception sites in Marsabit County, where teams are issuing blue wristbands with unique identification codes to document the arrivals. This process aims to establish an initial count of displaced individuals, including children, and will be followed by household profiling to assess needs and coordinate humanitarian aid. The influx has strained local resources, with many refugees seeking shelter in schools, churches, and camps. Humanitarian needs are significant, encompassing food, clean water, emergency shelter, and healthcare. The situation escalated following a dispute over the Somali Regional State flag and the tragic killing of a young girl, leading to heavy gunfire and civilian casualties. Humanitarian agencies have appealed for $8.9 million to support the response over the next three months.

ethiopia.title: Sudan Lodges Formal Complaints Against Ethiopia With UNSC, AU Peace and Security Council
ethiopia.content: Sudan Lodges Formal Complaints Against Ethiopia With UNSC, AU Peace and Security Council - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Sudan Lodges Formal Complaints Against Ethiopia With UNSC, AU Peace and Security Council 3 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Sudan's army-aligned government has lodged formal complaints against Ethiopia with the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) and the African Union Peace and Security Council (AUPSC), accusing the country of allowing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to use Ethiopian territory to launch drone attacks against Sudan. The complaints, publicly announced around November 1-2, allege that the RSF has used Ethiopian territory as a launch platform for one-way attack drones, some equipped with missiles, targeting Sudanese locations since February 2026. Sudan described the alleged operations as hostile acts that violate its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and called on both international and continental bodies to take urgent action. According to Sudan's submissions, authorities documented 70 attacks involving 187 one-way attack drones launched from Ethiopian territory between mid-February and late October 2026. October alone reportedly accounted for 28 attacks involving 97 drones. Sudan's army-aligned authorities reported that the alleged attacks killed or wounded 484 civilians, while 176 Sudanese soldiers were killed and approximately 200 others wounded. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The reported targets included residential areas, hospitals, fuel facilities and critical infrastructure, particularly power stations. Sudan said approximately 13 to 14 power stations had been hit across several states, including Khartoum, El Gezira, Sennar and El Gedaref, causing electricity outages and disrupting essential services. One incident cited in the complaints was an October 9 strike on displaced families in Wad el-Mahi, in the Blue Nile region near the Ethiopian border. Sudanese authorities said the attack killed 30 civilians, including 26 women and four children, and wounded approximately 100 others. Reports accompanying or referenced in the complaints identified Asosa Airport in western Ethiopia, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area and Bahir Dar airbase in the Amhara region as locations allegedly used to facilitate the drone operations. Sudan said it had submitted supporting documentation, including detailed tables outlining the reported attacks, types of drones used and resulting casualties and damage. Sudan argued that the alleged use of Ethiopian territory to launch attacks violates international law, including Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. In its appeals to the UNSC and AUPSC, Sudan called for explicit condemnation of the alleged attacks and urgent measures to ensure compliance with the UN Charter, African Union instruments and international law. It also urged the two bodies to help safeguard Sudan's sovereignty, prevent further attacks and hold those responsible accountable. Minister of Defense, Mohamed Idris made the remarks during talks with Chinese Ambassador to Ethiopia Chen Hai in Addis Ababa today, where the two sides discussed ways to expand cooperation in the defense industry, technology transfer, and military training. The also agreed to further consolidate their longstanding and productive military ties and elevate bilateral strategic cooperation to a higher level. Minister Mohamed emphasized the importance of sustaining the historic military partnership between the two countries while exploring expanded areas of collaboration, particularly in defense industrial development, technology transfer, and capacity-building through training opportunities. He also underscored that Ethiopia's efforts to safeguard its national interests contribute to regional and international peace and stability, calling on China to continue standing alongside Ethiopia. On his part, Ambassador Chen Hai reaffirmed China's interest in further deepening military and strategic ties with Ethiopia, ENA learned. The Ambassador also expressed China's readiness to expand cooperation in the defense industry, highlighting the positive outcomes already achieved through investment and bilateral engagement. ethiopia.title: When a Bull Falls for a Donkey - What an Unlikely Relationship Reveals About Animal Sexuality
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: When a Bull Falls for a Donkey - What an Unlikely Relationship Reveals About Animal Sexuality - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: When a Bull Falls for a Donkey - What an Unlikely Relationship Reveals About Animal Sexuality 2 November 2026 The Conversation Africa (Johannesburg) analysis By Jo Setchell On an Ethiopian plateau, a bull called Achille formed an unusual relationship with a male donkey named Patroclo. They were observed spending time together, licking and rubbing against one another, and repeatedly having penetrative sex. The animals' names nod to Achilles and Patroclus , the Greek mythological figures whose bond has been debated for thousands of years: devoted friends - or lovers? A new study in the journal Current Biology asks something similar about Achille and Patroclo: why would two males of different species repeatedly choose each other as sexual partners when females of their own species are available? Perhaps the more interesting question is why we find their relationship so surprising. A chance find Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The researchers first noticed Achille and Patroclo while studying gelada monkeys in Ethiopia. Intrigued, they began observing the pair more closely. They recorded 51 mounting attempts, 34 of which involved penetration. Patroclo took an active role, presenting his hindquarters to Achille and initiating contact. Unlike another male donkey that Achille approached, Patroclo did not show obvious signs of trying to avoid him. The donkey and bull often showed affection towards each other immediately after mounting. This suggests that sex may help strengthen their bond. The researchers observed the pair in detail for just four days, so they cannot say how long the relationship lasted. Even so, the findings are unusual because the two animals are both male and belong to different species. Same-sex sexual behaviour has been reported in more than 1,500 animal species. A 2023 study documented it in 261 mammalian species and found that it was particularly associated with social species, suggesting a possible role in maintaining relationships and managing conflict. As a primatologist, I am not surprised by these findings. Bonobos, for example, are famous for their frequent sexual interactions, which occur in many combinations of partners. Female-female genital rubbing, for instance, is associated with affiliation and social bonding. Sexual interactions can also help manage social tensions. Same-sex sexual behaviour takes many forms. Male bottlenose dolphins mount one another and rub genitals in groups that cooperate to gain access to females, while female Japanese macaques form temporary sexual partnerships involving repeated mounting. Same-sex sexual behaviour may play a part in establishing status, settling disputes, forming friendships or sexual enjoyment. Sexual behaviour between different species is rarer, but it is not unheard of. Both male and female Japanese macaques, for example, mount sika deer. Unlike the apparently reciprocal relationship between Achille and Patroclo, these encounters do not necessarily involve mutual sexual interest. What makes Achille and Patroclo particularly interesting is that they combine sexual activity with apparent affection and a preference for each other. Evolutionary biologists have traditionally approached same-sex sexual behaviour as a puzzle. If natural selection favours traits that contribute to reproductive success, why should animals spend time and energy engaging in sexual behaviour that cannot directly produce offspring? Suggested explanations include mistaken identity, a lack of opposite-sex partners, or indiscriminate sexual behaviour with whichever individuals happen to be nearby. But all these explanations begin with an assumption that sexual behaviour between males and females is the default, and same-sex behaviour represents a departure from it. In a provocative 2019 paper , a team of researchers challenged this assumption. They proposed that the ancestors of sexually reproducing animals may have been relatively indiscriminate about the sex of their sexual partners. Rather than assuming that different-sex sexual behaviour came first, they suggested that the ability to distinguish between potential partners, and preferentially direct sexual behaviour towards the opposite sex, may have evolved later. Taking a queer perspective This is a brilliant example of how queer perspectives can enrich evolutionary biology. Queer approaches encourage scientists to examine how human assumptions about sex, gender and sexuality influence the questions we ask, the categories we use and the explanations we consider plausible. They do not require us to assign human sexual identities to animals. Observing same-sex sexual behaviour does not tell us that an animal is gay or establish a fixed sexual orientation. Instead, queer approaches encourage us to take the diversity of animal sexual behaviour seriously, without assuming what is normal or what needs explaining. The authors of the new study suggest that Achille and Patroclo's sexual interactions may help maintain their social relationship. They also discuss the possible reproductive costs of spending time and energy on sexual activity that cannot result in offspring. Why should we assume that sexual behaviour must contribute directly to reproduction to have evolutionary significance? Social relationships can influence survival, access to resources and future reproductive opportunities. Sexual behaviour that strengthens those relationships may therefore have adaptive benefits, even when it cannot directly produce offspring. Equally, sexual behaviour may arise from evolved mechanisms without every individual encounter necessarily providing an animal's reproductive success. Achille and Patroclo cannot tell us why they choose one another. This short study can't tell us what evolutionary purpose, if any, their relationship serves. But it does remind us that animal behaviour can be more diverse than our theories suggest. Perhaps the most important lesson is not that a bull and a donkey have formed an unusual sexual relationship. It is that understanding such relationships requires us to question our assumptions about what sex is, what it does, and what counts as natural. Observations revealed that the two animals engaged in affectionate behaviors, including licking and rubbing, alongside repeated penetrative sexual acts. This relationship mirrors the bond of Achilles and Patroclus from Greek mythology, prompting researchers to explore why these two males of different species would choose each other over available females. The researchers argue that understanding such relationships challenges traditional views on animal sexuality and encourages a broader perspective on the evolutionary significance of sexual behavior, suggesting that it may not always be directly linked to reproduction but could instead enhance social connections and survival.

Sudan's military has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of aiding the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which it has been fighting since April 2023, including through drone attacks launched from Ethiopian territory. "The use of Ethiopian territory by the terrorist militia (RSF) to target Sudanese territory is considered a hostile act that places Ethiopia in violation of international law," it said. The attacks targeted residential complexes, hospitals and power and fuel stations, according to the report. In recent months, both the army and the RSF have increasingly relied on drones capable of striking targets hundreds of kilometres (miles) away without risking harm to their fighters. More than 1,100 people were killed in drone attacks across Sudan during the first half of the year, according to the United Nations. Recent attacks on power stations in areas controlled by the army have caused widespread electricity outages in the states of Khartoum, Al-Jazirah, White Nile and Gedaref. National Security and Ethiopia’s Russian Arms Deal: Strategic Interests and the Pressure of Sanctions Last updated: November 3, 2026 10:36 pm Marwa El- Shinawy Share 9 Min Read Dr Marwa El-Shinawy SHARE On 28 October 2026, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced from Moscow, on the sidelines of the Russia–Africa Summit, that Ethiopia had received 12 Su-35 fighter jets and would subsequently take delivery of four batteries of the S-400 air defence system. He thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for expediting the deliveries by a full year ahead of the originally agreed schedule, describing the development as a milestone in strengthening Ethiopia’s capacity for “preventive deterrence”. However, factual precision requires an important distinction. Rosoboronexport, Russia’s state arms exporter, confirmed to Reuters that the initial delivery arriving that day consisted of only two aircraft. Neither the financial value of the agreement nor the full delivery schedule for the remaining fighters, nor the anticipated delivery dates or deployment locations of the S-400 systems, has been publicly disclosed. The announcement therefore signals a significant arms agreement and the commencement of deliveries, but it does not mean that all the details are yet known. The deal did not emerge in a geopolitical vacuum. Ethiopia is grappling with renewed fighting in Tigray, an insurgency in Amhara, and escalating tensions with Eritrea. Against this backdrop, modernising its air force and air defence capabilities is a logical move from Addis Ababa’s perspective. For Russia, meanwhile, the agreement offers both financial returns and an opportunity to expand its strategic influence in the Horn of Africa, at a time when Moscow is seeking to preserve its share of African arms markets despite mounting Western sanctions. This is where Egypt’s concerns come into focus. In 2018, Cairo itself signed an agreement to purchase Russian Su-35 fighter jets in a deal estimated at approximately $2 billion and involving more than 20 aircraft. The agreement, however, encountered explicit warnings from Washington under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA). The United States cautioned that proceeding with the purchase could expose Egypt to sanctions that might undermine its extensive military cooperation with Washington, including its F-16 fleet, training programmes, and access to spare parts. Ultimately, the Egyptian deal fell through, and the aircraft never entered service with the Egyptian Air Force. Today, Ethiopia is acquiring the very same fighter aircraft, alongside plans to obtain the S-400 system, without any comparable public display of American pressure or announcement of sanctions—at least so far. This discrepancy raises a legitimate and straightforward question: Why did Egypt face intense American pressure to prevent its Su-35 purchase, while Ethiopia has not, to date, encountered similar pressure? The answer is far from straightforward. CAATSA does not operate automatically. Rather, it grants the US administration considerable discretion in determining whether a particular transaction with Russia’s defence sector constitutes a “significant transaction” warranting sanctions. Egypt’s military establishment has historically relied heavily on American-made systems, meaning that sanctions could have affected an extensive network of military cooperation and assistance. Ethiopia, by contrast, has a less deeply integrated military relationship with the United States and is less dependent on American military equipment. Consequently, the potential costs of applying pressure on Addis Ababa differ considerably from those associated with pressuring Cairo, at least from Washington’s perspective. Moreover, the United States may be approaching Ethiopia’s military modernisation through a different strategic lens, taking into account the country’s internal challenges and evolving regional dynamics. This does not mean that the Ethiopian deal is immune to potential future consequences. It does, however, demonstrate that different countries operate within different geopolitical and strategic calculations. From a military standpoint, the Su-35 fighters introduce additional operational capabilities into the Ethiopian Air Force, while the S-400 system, if delivered and fully integrated, would significantly strengthen Ethiopia’s long-range air defence architecture. Yet the value of any weapons system cannot be measured by its technical specifications alone. Operational readiness, pilot and personnel training, maintenance infrastructure, and integration with existing military platforms are equally critical factors. At present, there is insufficient evidence to establish that the agreement is specifically directed against Egypt or that it forms part of a broader strategy to exert pressure on Cairo over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). Nevertheless, it would be equally unwise to dismiss the significance of any military development capable of altering the regional balance of power in a strategic environment of such profound importance to Egyptian national security. This brings us to the problem of public statements intended to reassure Egyptian opinion. On 29 October 2026, the director of the Russian Federal News Network (RFN) stated that Ethiopia’s acquisition of these weapons did not mean they were intended to target Egypt. He argued that possessing advanced military equipment was fundamentally different from having the actual operational capacity to deploy it effectively, and emphasised that the S-400 was primarily a defensive system. He concluded by asserting that “Egyptian national security is closely intertwined with Russian national security”, adding that the two countries were moving along a shared path. The statement was published in a report by See News under a headline addressing the implications of the arms deal for Egyptian national security. Such remarks may reflect Moscow’s desire to preserve its bilateral relationship with Cairo. However, they do not constitute a binding Russian commitment to protect Egyptian interests in the event of any future Ethiopian military development. Nor do they explain how Moscow would respond if its interests in Egypt came into conflict with those it pursues in Ethiopia. Russia is perfectly capable of maintaining military partnerships with both Cairo and Addis Ababa simultaneously, according to its own strategic calculations. This is not necessarily an act of betrayal; rather, it reflects the fundamental nature of international relations, which are governed by evolving national interests rather than a permanent alignment of priorities. The real test of any strategic partnership is therefore not the warmth of diplomatic rhetoric, but the clarity of mutual interests and the ability of both parties to manage disagreements when security developments directly affect the vital interests of either side. For Egypt, the appropriate response is neither to turn the agreement into a diplomatic crisis with Russia nor to interpret it as definitive evidence of a conspiracy against Egyptian interests. Instead, Cairo needs to closely monitor the implementation of the deal, independently assess its actual military implications, and engage Moscow in a candid dialogue regarding its broader regional consequences. More importantly, Egypt must draw lessons from its own experience with the Su-35 deal. Its defence procurement strategy should be based on independent, long-term strategic calculations that carefully balance the diversification of arms suppliers, lifecycle and operating costs, interoperability between military systems, exposure to sanctions, and the preservation of strategic autonomy in national decision-making. Russia’s arms deal with Ethiopia does not prove that Moscow has abandoned Egypt, nor does it establish that Cairo is facing an immediate direct military threat. It does, however, reveal a deeper strategic reality: Egyptian national interests cannot be safeguarded by relying on declarations of friendship or assuming that the priorities of strategic partners will always coincide. They must instead be protected through accurate intelligence, independent strategic assessment, and diplomacy capable of distinguishing between issues that can be resolved through negotiation and those that require independent national preparedness. Between exaggerating the deal into a conspiracy against Egypt and dismissing its significance on the assumption that relations with Moscow are sufficient to contain its implications lies the space in which sound Egyptian decision-making must operate: a realistic assessment that neither exaggerates the threat nor offers reassurance unsupported by evidence. This development raises concerns for Egypt, which previously faced U.S. pressure that halted its own purchase of Su-35s due to potential sanctions under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA). The disparity in U.S. responses to the two nations stems from Egypt's deep military ties with the U.S., making sanctions more impactful, while Ethiopia's military relationship is less integrated. The article emphasizes that while the arms deal does not explicitly threaten Egypt, it could alter the regional balance of power. Egypt is urged to monitor the situation closely and engage in dialogue with Russia to safeguard its national interests, highlighting the need for a strategic approach to defense procurement that considers diverse suppliers and operational readiness.

Business Politics Interviews Culture Opinion Sports Lifestyle Follow US Opinion Politics Opinion | Ethiopia’s Illusions Last updated: November 3, 2026 10:14 pm Hatem Sadek Share 7 Min Read SHARE Would possessing 12 Su-35 fighter jets and four S-400 air defence batteries be enough for Ethiopia to alter the balance of power in the Horn of Africa or the Red Sea—even if those numbers were doubled? Some may argue that Russia’s direct involvement alone would be sufficient to bring about such a shift. The reality, however, is considerably more complex. This region is already saturated with foreign military bases, strategic alliances, and security arrangements, owing to its exceptional geostrategic significance and its proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, through which a substantial share of global trade and oil shipments passes. Djibouti is arguably the country hosting the largest concentration of foreign military bases in the world, owing to its unique location overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It hosts American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and Italian military bases, as well as European military contingents from Germany and Spain. Somalia, meanwhile, hosts three military bases operated by the United States, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates. In Eritrea, Israel maintains intelligence and electronic surveillance facilities. Moscow has also concluded security agreements and understandings with Asmara concerning the use of facilities at the Port of Massawa. Russia, moreover, relies on an informal military presence and private security contractors, such as the Africa Corps and its predecessor, the Wagner Group, to expand its influence on the ground. These entities have been involved in providing security and military services, as well as training, in Sudan and neighbouring African countries. As for regional military and security alliances, the African Union and the United Nations provide an institutional framework aimed at supporting the Somali government and combating the Al-Shabaab militant group. This effort involves forces from neighbouring and other African countries, including Uganda, Burundi, Kenya, Djibouti, and Ethiopia. There is also the Council of Arab and African States Bordering the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, established through a regional initiative to strengthen cooperation and security among countries bordering the Red Sea. Its membership includes Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, Sudan, Djibouti, Somalia, and Eritrea. The council is intended to serve as a framework for political and security coordination in confronting maritime threats and external interference. Prof. Hatem Sadek On another front, Israeli news outlets have been promoting the argument that this arms acquisition—12 Su-35 fighter jets—is sufficient to constrain Egypt’s ability to launch a strike against the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). Yet even if the number of aircraft were increased, the decisive factor would remain not the weapons themselves, but the ability to deploy them effectively and operate them successfully. According to information cited by specialized military sources, including Global Firepower and the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), the distance between Egyptian military airbases and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam exceeds approximately 1,500 to 2,000 kilometres. Egypt’s Air Force operates Rafale, MiG-29, and F-16 fighter aircraft, supported by aerial refuelling tankers and long-range air-to-ground weapons, as well as cruise missiles such as the SCALP. These capabilities allow for the launch of missiles from safe stand-off distances, beyond the direct engagement range of air defence systems. Despite its considerable capabilities, the S-400 system requires full integration with a layered early-warning radar network and a comprehensive air defence architecture encompassing short-, medium-, and long-range systems. It must also be supported by capabilities designed to counter networked missile threats, extremely low-altitude targets, and electronic penetration. The system is by no means an impenetrable shield when operated in isolation or without comprehensive electronic warfare support. Any carefully planned aerial operation would employ aerial deception, electronic warfare, intensive jamming, and potentially the targeting of military bases and airfields from which Ethiopian fighter aircraft operate, either before or during the operation. Such measures could significantly reduce the effectiveness of those aircraft in intercepting incoming threats. The Egyptian military establishment possesses decades of experience in developing integrated air defence networks, conducting complex air operations (COMAO), and employing electronic jamming and electronic warfare capabilities. This constitutes a decisive advantage in any tactical or strategic confrontation. Ultimately, the decisive factor in determining whether such an operation succeeds or fails is not the number of weapons systems Ethiopia possesses. Rather, success depends on the operational scenario, intelligence capabilities, and the degree of integration between electronic warfare and military planning. Interestingly, according to a report published by the Israeli website NZIV, the aircraft acquired by Ethiopia are Su-35E fighters originally manufactured for Egypt. Cairo had reportedly cancelled the deal after redirecting its procurement strategy toward the more advanced Rafale fighter. Moscow subsequently concluded the agreement with Addis Ababa because it was seeking “ready buyers” for aircraft that had already been manufactured, while also seeking to avoid disrupting production lines allocated to its own armed forces amid the war in Ukraine. In conclusion, claims that Russia’s arms deal with Ethiopia is capable of fundamentally altering the balance of power in the Horn of Africa or curtailing Egypt’s regional role amount to little more than wishful thinking. The concentration of foreign military bases, the overlapping network of strategic interests, and the extraordinary complexity of the regional landscape make it highly unlikely that 12 fighter jets and four S-400 air defence batteries could single-handedly turn the strategic equation upside down. The possibilities, therefore, remain largely confined to two scenarios: either Addis Ababa is seeking limited domestic propaganda gains to boost public morale without generating any meaningful strategic impact, or the deal may contribute to a temporary escalation in military tensions without giving Ethiopia the ability to impose a fundamentally new balance of power. The broader strategic realities, including the major regional power dynamics and established international alliances, remain firmly in place—and are unlikely to be fundamentally altered by arms acquisitions of such limited scale. ethiopia.summary: In the opinion piece "Ethiopia’s Illusions," Prof. Hatem Sadek discusses the implications of Ethiopia's recent military acquisitions, specifically 12 Su-35 fighter jets and four S-400 air defense systems from Russia. He argues that these additions are unlikely to significantly alter the balance of power in the Horn of Africa or the Red Sea, a region already saturated with foreign military bases and strategic alliances. Sadek highlights that while Ethiopia may seek to bolster its military image domestically, the complexities of regional dynamics, including established military capabilities and alliances, will limit any substantial impact from these acquisitions. He emphasizes that effective military operations depend more on operational planning, intelligence, and integration of electronic warfare than on sheer numbers of weapons. Ultimately, he concludes that claims of a fundamental shift in power dynamics due to Ethiopia's arms deal are largely exaggerated, suggesting that the deal may only lead to temporary escalations in military tensions without altering the strategic landscape.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Retakes Rebel Stronghold in Tigray While Seeking to Stabilize Security Situation - Black Agenda Report
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Retakes Rebel Stronghold in Tigray While Seeking to Stabilize Security Situation | Black Agenda Report Black Agenda Report News, commentary and analysis from the black left. Donate Home Africa African America Education Environment International Media and Culture Political Economy Radio US Politics War and Empire Search Search Ethiopia Retakes Rebel Stronghold in Tigray While Seeking to Stabilize Security Situation Abayomi Azikiwe 04 Nov 2026 🖨️ Print Article Ethiopian soldiers retaking more areas in the Tigray region. Armed opposition groups have failed to make gains as the capital, Addis Ababa, remains firmly under government control. Originally published in Fighting Words . During September a group of armed opposition groups from various regions of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia declared that they would wage a war to seize power from Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and the ruling Prosperity Party. However, several weeks later the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) took control of the capital of the Tigray province resulting in the armed opposition group to abandon the capital of Mekelle. The ENDF marched into Mekelle without any political or armed resistance from the then ruling Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and its military wing, the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF). Although the TDF says that it abandoned its stronghold of Mekelle it claims that they will continue their fight outside of Mekelle. As the TPLF fled the ENDF, another grouping aligned with the government in Addis Ababa, the Tigray Peace Forces (TPF), moved into Mekelle to take control of the day-to-day security issues. The TPF is a manifestation of the split within the opposition TPLF which occurred in the aftermath of the Pretoria Peace Agreement of 2022. Many believe that the events of the last few months have effectively destroyed this peace agreement which was facilitated by several key members of the African Union (AU), primarily South Africa and Kenya. The negotiations which brought an end to the war between the TPLF based in Tigray and the central government in Addis Ababa was championed at the time as a prime example of the AU creating solutions to African problems. However, the joint statement issued by the opposition groupings in September which called themselves the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival (EPFAS) articulated no imminent threats which would warrant the initiation of a civil war. The groups which were encompassed in this coalition are the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF); Oromo Liberation Army (OLA); Amhara Fano National Movement (Fano); Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF); Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF/ANURF); and the Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement (BPLM). Several of these organizations historically have been in extreme conflict with each other. Within this reality, what is the basis of the alliance of these regional groupings? Although these rebel groups have stated that their aim is to overthrow the central government there is no firm explanation as to how they differ politically from Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The TPLF which ruled the country from 1991-2018 after the collapse of the Ethiopia Worker’s Party under Col. Mengistu Haile Mariam, led a coalition called the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) that waged a war for the overthrow of the EWP. The ascendancy of the TPLF-EPRDF was heavily impacted by the disintegration of the Soviet Union and the Socialist states in Eastern Europe which had supported the then Ethiopian government. A national rebellion during 2018 brought about the rise of Prime Minister Abiy. The Abiy government during 2018 signed a peace accord with neighboring Eritrea ending a war which had lasted for nearly two decades. However, in recent years relations with the State of Eritrea have deteriorated. Eritrea had been in congruence with the Ethiopian government when the TPLF-led province attempted to succeed from the authority of the central administration in Addis Ababa. After the defeat of the TPLF and the adoption of the Pretoria Agreement in 2022, tensions surfaced over the calls by Abiy for access to the Eritrean port at Massawa. Battlefield Reports from Tigray and Beyond There have been reports of the defection of a leading figure within the TPLF. This compounds the internal splits inside the leading opposition rebel grouping. According to a Substack post on the situation among the TPLF, it notes: “The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) has accused senior military commander Maj. Gen. Yohannes Woldegiorgis, also known as John Medid, of defecting to the Ethiopian Federal Government and disclosing military secrets. The accusation came a day after the pro-government Tigray Peace Force, which is allied with the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), confirmed that the general was in government custody. In a statement, the TPLF faction led by Debretsion Gebremichael alleged that Yohannes had refused to participate in an internal military evaluation before defecting with a small group of associates. The group further accused him of establishing contacts with the Federal Government and sharing sensitive military information.” Other reports from the battlefield suggest that the alliance of armed opposition groupings have failed to make gains in their efforts to seize power inside Ethiopia. In a series of articles and a briefing from the Ethiopian military, the rebels have been halted in their military operations. An Associated Press report published by the United States based ABC News says of the present situation that: “An official in Tigray’s new federal-backed administration urged rebel fighters to lay down their weapons Friday, hours after a rebel commander called for continued resistance despite losing the northern Ethiopian region’s capital. The calls came nearly three weeks after rebels trying to overthrow the government lost control of Mekelle, Tigray’s capital. Government-allied fighters entered Mekelle on Oct. 4 after the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, withdrew. Redae Halefom Woldeselassie, the caretaker administration’s chief executive for political and public mobilization, said rebel forces were collapsing and urged fighters to enter a disarmament and reintegration program. ‘This is not the time for settling scores, I call upon you to return to your homes and continue your civilian lives,’ he said in Mekelle. He dismissed the prospect of the rebels retaking the city and portrayed the conflict as serving a small group of leaders rather than the people of Tigray.” Meanwhile, the Ethiopia government has announced that they have received the first batch of Su-35 fighter jets from the Russian Federation. The SU-35s will be accompanied by a number of S-400s as well which are designed to bolster their national security. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed noted that the jets were delivered a year earlier than anticipated, saying that this was done due to Moscow’s concern over the security of the Horn of Africa state which is the headquarters of the 55 member-states AU in Addis Ababa. This announcement came on the eve of the convening of the Russia-Africa Summit on October 27-28 in Moscow. Additional reports of refugees fleeing from Ethiopia into Kenya at Moyale is the result of conflicts between residents of the regional states of Oromia and Somalia. This displacement appears not to be connected with the rebel insurgents seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy. Status of the Renewed Tensions with Eritrea There have been several news articles claiming that Eritrean troops have been sighted on the border areas with Ethiopia during mid-October. However, there have not been any confirmed reports of serious fighting between the two states. The Russian Federation has offered to serve as a neutral location for mediation talks between Addis Ababa and Asmara. This offer was renewed during the Russia-Africa Summit. A regional summit was held in Egypt during early October which excluded the Ethiopian government. Those present were the leaders of Sudan, Somalia and Eritrea. The meeting participants issued a joint statement, yet no further reports on the results of the gathering have been released. Egypt has opposed the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) project which President Abdel-Fattah al-Sisi says would undermine the country’s water supply. However, it was British colonialism which established the current arrangements involving the Nile Rivers aimed at benefiting Egypt at the expense of Ethiopia. There can be no benefit to the people of the Horn of Africa if a full-scale war erupts in Ethiopia prompting widespread dislocation, injuries and deaths. The offer to mediate by the Russian Federation could provide an opening for the normalization of relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea in the near future. Abayomi Azikiwe is the Editor of Pan-African News Wire . He is a Research Associate of the Centre for Research on Globalization (CRG). ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian forces have regained control of Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, as armed opposition groups struggle to mount a significant challenge against the government led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) took over Mekelle without resistance from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has since vowed to continue its fight outside the city. The TPLF's retreat has led to the emergence of the Tigray Peace Forces (TPF), which now manages local security. The recent developments have raised concerns about the viability of the 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement, which aimed to resolve the conflict between the TPLF and the central government. Meanwhile, reports indicate internal strife within the TPLF, including defections of key military figures. The Ethiopian government has also received military support from Russia, further complicating the regional security landscape, as tensions with Eritrea persist.

Indian Navy rescues hijacked fishing vessel off Somalia, frees 20 crew Listen to this article 0.75x 1x 1.5x 00:00 / 00:00 New Delhi, Nov 3: The Indian Navy has rescued a hijacked fishing vessel, Azini, from armed pirates off the coast of Somalia following an operation lasting over 48 hours, securing the safe release of all 20 crew members without any casualties or injuries. Advertisment According to the Defence Ministry, the vessel was hijacked by an armed pirate group off the north-eastern coast of Somalia last month. The hijacking posed a serious maritime security threat, as the vessel could have been used as a ‘mother ship’ to launch further attacks on merchant vessels in the region. The Indian Navy deployed a mission-ready warship, supported by a maritime reconnaissance aircraft, to locate and intercept the vessel. Through persistent surveillance and coordinated action, the naval platforms tracked its movements and used calibrated non-kinetic measures to restrict its movement and prevent it from escaping. Marine Commandos were also reinforced through a precision airdrop by an Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft. The commandos subsequently carried out a swift tactical operation, secured the vessel and overcame the pirate threat, enabling the release of all 20 crew members. Advertisment The Navy said the successful operation demonstrated its operational preparedness and the ability of the armed forces to conduct complex maritime security missions through close inter-service coordination. The operation also reaffirmed India’s commitment to acting as a “First Responder” and “Preferred Security Partner” in the Indian Ocean Region, the Navy said, adding that it remained committed to protecting seafarers, securing vital maritime trade routes and maintaining a safe and stable maritime environment. by GK NEWS SERVICE by GK NEWS SERVICE 04 Nov 2026 07:32 IST Link copied! The vessel was seized by armed pirates last month, raising significant maritime security concerns as it could have been used to launch further attacks on merchant ships. In response, the Indian Navy deployed a warship and a maritime reconnaissance aircraft to track the vessel. Through coordinated efforts and non-kinetic measures, they restricted the pirates' movements. Marine Commandos were then deployed via a precision airdrop from an Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft. They executed a tactical operation that neutralized the pirate threat and secured the vessel without any casualties. This operation highlights the Indian Navy's readiness and capability to conduct complex maritime security missions, reaffirming India's role as a key security partner in the Indian Ocean Region and its commitment to safeguarding maritime trade routes.

The operation lasted more than 48 hours and ended in the Arabian Sea. India’s Defense Ministry announced the rescue Tuesday. Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said the crew’s boat, the Azini, was recovered Monday more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai. Suspects disarmed and released An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force said Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, took their mobile phones and then released them. The official spoke anonymously because he was not authorized to address the media. The suspects and two Somali security guards later reached Bandar Bayla, in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three people who came ashore had minor injuries. The official did not identify whether they were among the suspected pirates or the guards, or explain how they were hurt. Advertisement India’s ministry said the operation concluded without casualties or injuries. The statement left unclear whether that description referred to everyone involved or only the rescued crew. What is known about the rescue The accounts confirm that the vessel had been hijacked off Somalia and that Indian forces freed the boat and its 20 crew. They do not describe how the navy found the Azini or the tactics used during the operation. The location of the hijacking and the identities of the suspected pirates were also not specified. Read also Ballot Scanner Failure Disrupts Voting in New York House Battleground That distinction matters: the Puntland official described 12 people as suspected pirates, while the Indian ministry reported the successful rescue. The claims about disarmament and the suspects’ release come from the local maritime police official; India’s account focused on the operation and its outcome. The incident involved a fishing vessel linked to Iran, Indian naval forces operating in the Arabian Sea and suspected Somali pirates who later landed in Puntland. For the crew, the immediate stakes were direct: their boat had been seized, and their release followed an operation that ran for more than two days. For authorities, the arrival of the suspects and guards at Bandar Bayla adds a local dimension to a rescue carried out at sea. Advertisement The reported details leave the crew’s condition central to what happens next. India’s ministry said there were no injuries, while the Puntland official separately reported minor injuries among three people who came ashore. He did not say whether those injured were guards or suspects. India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said the rescue was completed in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers from Mumbai. somalia.title: Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 3, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia produces about 30,000 tonnes of fish annually, just 5% of its estimated marine fishery production capacity of 600,000 tonnes, according to a report by The EastAfrican, as the country seeks to attract investment into its underdeveloped fishing industry. Abdi Dirshe, director general of Somalia's Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy, said the gap between current output and estimated capacity stands at nearly 570,000 tonnes a year. Dirshe estimated that the sector could generate between $1.8 billion and $3 billion in annual revenue and create more than 210,000 jobs if its resources were properly developed. The figures represent potential economic returns rather than existing industry revenue or employment. Somalia has approximately 3,333 kilometres of coastline, but inadequate fishing equipment, limited processing and storage facilities, and security concerns have restricted the industry's development. Investment and fisheries policy Expanding production would require investment in fishing vessels, equipment, landing sites, cold storage, processing plants and export infrastructure. Abdullahi Adan, coordinator of Somalia's Sustainable Fisheries Development Project, known as Badmaal, said the government's National Transformation Plan 2025–2029 prioritises private investment, market development and public-private partnerships in the sector. Somalia has introduced legal and regulatory measures intended to encourage investment, including an Investment Law, a public-private partnership policy, a Fisheries Law and food safety regulations. Local companies have also begun investing in fish processing and boatbuilding, with projects aimed at creating jobs and developing technical skills among young Somalis. Export markets and security challenges Engineer Ali Ibrahim Siyad, chairman of the Somali Fish Exporters Association, said quality assurance and seafood certification are essential for gaining access to international markets. He identified the United States, China, the Middle East and East African countries as potential destinations for Somali fish exports. However, exporters face difficulties meeting the requirements of international markets, while the industry continues to operate with limited infrastructure and equipment. Fisheries expert Omar Abdulle Hayle said security remains the primary consideration for investors seeking to protect their personnel and assets. The report also identified limited capacity to protect marine resources as an obstacle to developing the industry. Fisheries experts called for transparent management and stronger marine environmental protection alongside efforts to increase production. AUSSOM Photo/Mahamud Hassan SHARE Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Mogadishu (Somalia Today) — African Union peacekeepers plan to take over four bases near Mogadishu as Uganda withdraws troops from Somalia, according to a mission letter obtained by the Associated Press . The African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia, or AUSSOM, would occupy Sabid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle and Bulonagad during November troop rotations. Its October 31 letter to the UN support office describes the positions as critical to the capital’s security, AP reported. The troops would be redeployed from Barawe, a coastal town about 220 kilometres southwest of Mogadishu. It remains unclear who would secure the positions they leave behind. “Things are not dire now, but it could create problems if their troops suddenly pull out,” Ali Omar, Somalia’s state minister for foreign affairs, told Reuters . Uganda announced on Monday that it had begun withdrawing troops deployed under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It said all its forces, including those serving with AUSSOM, would leave by the end of 2027. Military spokesman Colonel Chris Magezi said the first group had already returned to Uganda. “The operation to withdraw troops deployed in Somalia under bilateral arrangements will be completed in the next few days,” he said in Monday’s statement. Uganda became the first country to contribute troops to the original AU mission in March 2007. Its planned departure would end two decades of operations supporting Somali forces against the insurgency. Lower Shabelle According to AP’s account of the letter, Uganda deployed the bilateral force after an April 2025 summit at which African leaders called for more troops to fight Al-Shabaab. The contingent helped recapture and hold territory over the following 17 months. Somali army commander Major General Ibrahim Mohamed Mohamud visited Barawe on Monday and ordered troops to remain alert and step up operations against Al-Shabaab, the army said. Its statement did not say whether Somali soldiers would take over the AU positions. Somali and AU forces captured Barawe from Al-Shabaab in 2014. The militants had used its port to bring in fighters and weapons and export charcoal to raise money. The Al-Qaeda-linked group continues to attack military and civilian targets despite successive international deployments and Somali offensives. Last week, an officer who survived an ambush in the Bay region told AP that the militants had killed at least 20 Somali soldiers. The government acknowledged damage to military vehicles but gave no troop casualty figures. Funding uncertainty Funding shortages had accelerated the withdrawal, Farhan Isak Yusuf, deputy executive director of the Mogadishu-based research organisation Somali Public Agenda, told AP. He said the Somali army lacked resources and described Lower Shabelle, where the departing troops were stationed, as vital to protecting Mogadishu. Uganda’s military statement did not explain why the bilateral contingent was leaving immediately. AUSSOM’s current UN Security Council authorisation runs until December 31 and allows up to 11,826 uniformed personnel, including 680 police. The council has urged donors to provide the funding needed to carry out its mandate. The mission relies on the separate United Nations Support Office in Somalia, or UNSOS, for food, fuel, medical evacuation, transport and other logistical support. Washington said in September that it would stop funding or supporting UNSOS. The agency also reported , citing a diplomatic note, that the United States was willing to support a 12-month drawdown. Diplomatic and Somali government sources told Reuters the period would begin in January 2027. “We would expect any drawdown processes and timelines to be discussed during UN Security Council deliberations in December,” a US State Department spokesperson told Reuters. The decision gives Somalia, the African Union and international partners more time to find alternative funding and logistical arrangements for AUSSOM. The withdrawals come as Somalia takes on responsibilities previously handled by the UN’s political mission, which closed on October 31 after a two-year transition requested by the Somali government. The mission’s functions have passed to Somali institutions and UN agencies. Aid agencies remain in the country, while UNSOS continues to support AU peacekeepers and some Somali security forces. In a statement marking the political mission’s closure , UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for sustained international assistance, including support against Al-Shabaab and for a gradual security transition. This transition is part of the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which aims to maintain security in the capital, Mogadishu. Uganda's military announced that it has started the withdrawal process, with a complete exit expected by the end of 2027. The withdrawal raises concerns about the security vacuum left behind, particularly in Lower Shabelle, a region critical for protecting Mogadishu. Funding shortages have accelerated Uganda's departure, and the Somali army is urged to remain vigilant against Al-Shabaab, which continues to pose a threat despite international military efforts. The AU mission's current UN mandate allows for nearly 12,000 personnel, but funding and logistical support remain uncertain as the UN political mission in Somalia has recently closed.

somalia.title: Somalia, Djibouti national security inseparable: Somali's parliament speaker - TRT Afrika
somalia.content: Somalia, Djibouti national security inseparable: Somali's parliament speaker - TRT Afrika | English | English POLITICS AFRICA TÜRKİYE OPINION FEATURES SPORTS AFRICA 6 min read Somalia, Djibouti national security inseparable: Somali's parliament speaker Somalia’s parliament speaker praises Djibouti’s role in the rebuilding of Somalia, from the historic Arta peace conference to its military contribution to the fight against terrorism. Share Somalia’s parliament speaker Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur with Djibouti President Ismail Omar Guelleh By Nuri Aden Somalia’s parliament speaker said Tuesday that the security of Somalia cannot be considered separately from the security of Djibouti, calling for closer cooperation between the two neighbours as the Horn of Africa faces growing security tensions. Speaker Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur said the two countries shared a responsibility to protect their peace and stability. He made the remarks in an address to Djibouti’s parliamentarians during his first official visit abroad since taking office . “Djibouti’s security is our security, and Somalia’s security is Djibouti’s security,” Nur told lawmakers. The peace and stability of our two countries are a shared responsibility in which we are equal partners.” The speaker, also known as Jaamac, made the visit at the invitation of his Djibouti counterpart, Dileita Mohamed Dileita. Nur described the relationship between the two countries as one that extended beyond diplomacy, pointing to their shared history, family ties and Djibouti’s longstanding involvement in Somalia’s political recovery. ‘Twin nation’ “Let those who do not know Djibouti learn about it, and let there be no miscalculation. Djibouti is Somalia, and Somalia is Djibouti,” he said. “We are two countries, but we are twin nations, bound by brotherhood, blood and shared ancestry.” A central part of Nur’s address focused on Djibouti’s contribution to Somalia’s state-building efforts following the collapse of the central government in 1991. He recalled how Djibouti hosted reconciliation initiatives aimed at bringing Somali factions together, ending violence and restoring national institutions. Nur singled out the historic Arta peace conference, which paved the way for the establishment of Somalia’s Transitional National Government in 2000. The conference marked a significant step in efforts to restore Somali state institutions and re-establish the country’s political representation internationally after years of civil conflict. “When Somalia’s central government collapsed in 1991, Djibouti stepped forward to bring Somalis together, stop the bloodshed and rebuild our state,” Nur said. He credited Djiboutian President Ismail Omar Guelleh with playing an important role in those efforts. “Somalia remembers the support Djibouti extended to our country and the role President Ismail Omar Guelleh played in the restoration of the Somali state,” he said. Longstanding friend Nur described Guelleh as a longstanding friend and supporter of Somalia, saying the Somali people would continue to recognise Djibouti’s contribution to their country’s recovery. He also praised Djibouti’s subsequent efforts to mediate political disagreements among Somali groups and encourage dialogue between opposing sides. “The debt of gratitude we owe Djibouti is one that we carry with us. It is written in the memory of the Somali people, and it is our responsibility to pass that history on to future generations,” he said. Fight against terrorism Nur also paid tribute to Djibouti’s military contribution to Somalia’s security, particularly the Djiboutian troops serving alongside Somali forces in operations against terrorist groups. He said Djibouti’s support had gone beyond hosting peace conferences and diplomatic engagement, extending to direct military assistance during the rebuilding of Somalia’s security institutions. “Djibouti did not limit its support to peace conferences and diplomatic efforts. You sent your sons to stand with us in the difficult fight against terrorism and in defence of the peace and lives of the Somali people,” he said. The speaker expressed particular appreciation for Djiboutian troops serving on the front lines in Somalia. RECOMMENDED Former Nigeria governor loses $136m wealth seizure appeal in corruption case Ebola outbreak: Kenya discharges more patients after recovery Uganda's former deputy army chief arrested over 'destabilisation' plot South Sudan to recruit 10,000 police officers ahead of first-ever polls RECOMMENDED Former Nigeria governor loses $136m wealth seizure appeal in corruption case Ebola outbreak: Kenya discharges more patients after recovery Uganda's former deputy army chief arrested over 'destabilisation' plot South Sudan to recruit 10,000 police officers ahead of first-ever polls “The Somali people see your courage, appreciate your sacrifices and will never forget your solidarity,” Nur said, addressing Djiboutian military officers and soldiers deployed in Somalia. He also praised Djibouti’s diplomatic support for Somalia’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity at regional and international forums. Nur said Djibouti had maintained those positions despite the political, diplomatic and security challenges involved. Regional tensions Turning to developments in the Horn of Africa, Nur warned that the region was facing increasing competition, security tensions and challenges affecting the stability of neighbouring countries. He said those circumstances required Somalia and Djibouti to strengthen consultations, coordinate their responses and maintain close cooperation. “Our region is passing through a difficult period. Competition is intensifying, security tensions are increasing, and circumstances are emerging that affect the stability of our countries and the lives of our people,” he said. “This moment demands wisdom, vigilance and greater unity. We need to consult one another, remain closely coordinated and work together to overcome the challenges ahead.” Nur reiterated that Somalia regarded Djibouti’s security as directly linked to its own, describing peace and stability in both countries as a common responsibility. His remarks highlighted the importance Mogadishu places on its relationship with Djibouti as regional governments confront security and diplomatic challenges. Parliamentary diplomacy The Somali speaker also outlined plans to deepen cooperation between the two countries’ parliaments. Nur said he had deliberately chosen Djibouti as the destination for his first official visit to a foreign parliament since becoming speaker of Somalia’s House of the People. “Beginning my official parliamentary visits in Djibouti was a deliberate choice, reflecting the affection, respect and recognition of the brotherly support that binds our two countries,” he said. “I wanted my first step to bring me to this parliament and this country, which has played such an important role in Somalia’s recovery.” He called for closer cooperation between parliamentary committees, greater exchanges of legislative expertise and joint training opportunities for parliamentary staff. “We want our committees to work together, our lawmakers to exchange experience, and the staff of our two parliaments to benefit from joint training and knowledge-sharing,” Nur said. The speaker also highlighted the importance of parliamentary diplomacy in strengthening relations between the two governments and creating opportunities for cooperation that benefit their populations. A relationship rooted in shared historyNur concluded his address by thanking Djibouti’s government, parliament and people for their hospitality and longstanding support for Somalia. He said his visit was intended not only to strengthen institutional relations but also to renew the bonds of solidarity between the two countries. “We have come to thank you. We have come to renew our bond of brotherhood. We have come to deliver a message from the Somali people: Somalia remembers Djibouti’s support,” he said. The speaker expressed hope that the relationship would continue to develop through practical cooperation between the two parliaments. For Somalia, Nur’s address placed Djibouti’s role in the country’s political reconstruction, military security and diplomatic engagement at the centre of a partnership he said must remain strong as the Horn of Africa faces new challenges. Speaking to Djibouti's parliament, he highlighted Djibouti's critical role in Somalia's rebuilding efforts, particularly through the historic Arta peace conference and military support against terrorism. Nur stated, "Djibouti’s security is our security, and Somalia’s security is Djibouti’s security," underscoring their shared responsibility for peace and stability. Nur called for enhanced cooperation between the two nations, particularly in parliamentary diplomacy, to strengthen their ties and address regional security challenges. He concluded by expressing gratitude for Djibouti's longstanding support, reinforcing the notion that the two countries are "twin nations" bound by history and solidarity.

somalia.title: Somalia condemns Israeli envoy’s accreditation in breakaway Somaliland - Anadolu Ajansı
somalia.content: Skip to main content Reporting the Changing World CORPORATE History Executive Team Quality Management Editorial Guidelines Social Media Policies Logos Privacy and Cookies Policy Information Policy RSS Diary COMMUNICATION Contact Subscription Requests Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 WORLD TÜRKİYE ECONOMY POLITICS ENERGY TECHNOLOGY World Africa Somalia condemns Israeli envoy’s accreditation in breakaway Somaliland Move null, void, unity of Somali nation not negotiable, says Mogadishu Mohamed Dhaysane 03 November 2026 • Update : 03 November 2026 MOGADISHU, Somalia Somalia strongly condemned on Tuesday Israel’s “purported accreditation” of its ambassador in the breakaway region of Somaliland. Mogadishu said the Israeli move is null and void, and Somali national unity is not negotiable. A Foreign Ministry statement on Tel Aviv’s actions, undertaken without the consent of the Federal Government of Somalia, said it constitutes a flagrant violation of Somalia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and unity. Somalia rejects it as null and void and without legal effect. It said Hargeisa and the breakaway Somaliland region remain an integral and inseparable part of the Federal Republic of Somalia. “The establishment of diplomatic relations and permanent diplomatic missions requires the consent of the sovereign State, as provided for in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations,” it said. The ministry indicated that no unilateral act can bypass that requirement or alter the status of Somali territory. “These measures compound Israel's unlawful recognition of December 2025, already rejected by the African Union, IGAD (Intergovernmental Authority on Development), the League of Arab States and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation,” it added. The Foreign Ministry warned that amid heightened insecurity in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, actions that encourage fragmentation and disregard internationally recognized borders risk deepening tensions in an already fragile region. Mogadishu demanded that Israel “immediately” reverse the measures, and urged all states and international organizations to reject them and refrain from any engagement that would confer legitimacy upon them. It said the federal government reserves the right to employ all appropriate diplomatic, political and legal avenues under international law to defend the country's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. somalia.summary: Somalia has condemned Israel's recent accreditation of an ambassador to the breakaway region of Somaliland, declaring the move null and void. The Somali Foreign Ministry stated that this action, taken without the consent of the Federal Government, violates Somalia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It emphasized that Somaliland is an inseparable part of Somalia and that diplomatic relations require the approval of the sovereign state, as outlined in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. The ministry criticized Israel's actions as exacerbating tensions in a fragile region, especially amid ongoing insecurity in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Somalia called for Israel to reverse its decision and urged other nations and international organizations to reject any engagement that might legitimize this accreditation. The government affirmed its commitment to defending Somalia's sovereignty and unity through all appropriate diplomatic and legal means. (151 words)

football.summary: تستعرض يلاكورة مواعيد ونتائج مباريات دوري أبطال أفريقيا لموسم 2026/2027، حيث يتضمن جدول المباريات مجموعة من المواجهات المثيرة. من المقرر أن تبدأ الجولة الأولى من دور الـ32 في 22 يناير 2027، حيث يلتقي الهلال السوداني مع المغرب الفاسي، وسيمبا مع نادي كولومب، بالإضافة إلى مباريات أخرى تشمل الزمالك ضد مولودية الجزائر والترجي الرياضي ضد إف سي نواذيبو. كما يتم تسليط الضوء على الفرق المشاركة مثل الأفريقي التونسي، المريخ، والهلال السوداني، مع تقديم إحصائيات حول الهدافين وصانعي الأهداف. تتضمن المقالة أيضًا أخبارًا تتعلق بالفرق، مثل تعثر الأفريقي أمام الملعب التونسي، واستعدادات الزمالك لمواجهاته المقبلة. يهدف الموقع إلى توفير معلومات شاملة حول البطولة، بما في ذلك التحليلات والتقارير المتعلقة بالمباريات والفرق.

(winwin) 3 نوفمبر 2026 المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا الهلال السوداني المريخ دوري أبطال أفريقيا الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin عاد نجم نادي الهلال والمنتخب السوداني، مصطفى كرشوم، إلى الواجهة بقوة، مقدمًا مستويات مميزة في الآونة الأخيرة، إذ استعاد بريقه الكامل خلال مباراتي "صقور الجديان" في التصفيات الأفريقية، ومباريات فريقه في الدورين التمهيديين لمسابقة دوري أبطال أفريقيا . وقد أشعل المدافع المتألق سباقًا مبكرًا بين قطبي الكرة السودانية مع اقتراب دخوله "الفترة الحرة"، إذ يسعى النادي الأحمر لاستعادة نجمه السابق، بينما يتمسك "الأزرق" بجوهرته بعد أن وجد ضالته في المدافع الفذ، الذي يصنفه الخبراء بأنه أفضل لاعب في البلاد خلال السنوات الأخيرة. الهلال يتحرك للحفاظ على نجمه في هذا السياق، كشفت مصادر موثوقة لموقع "winwin" أن إدارة نادي الهلال استشعرت الخطر، وبدأت تحركاتها مبكرًا لتأمين بقاء نجمها وتمديد تعاقده قبل دخوله الفترة الحرة؛ وذلك بعد أن نجح اللاعب في إعادة الصلابة والهيبة لدفاع الفريق، الذي عانى من تذبذب واضح في مستوياته السابقة. ويعد كرشوم ظاهرة نادرة في الملاعب السودانية؛ نظرًا لسلوكه الاحترافي وانضباطه العالي، فضلًا عن ثبات مستواه وقلة أخطائه. وفي هذا الصدد، فتحت إدارة النادي برئاسة هشام السوباط باب التفاوض مع اللاعب؛ لضمان استمراره في صفوف الفريق لمدة عامين إضافيين على الأقل. اقرأ أيضًا اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص خاص | نجم السودان يفتح النار ويشرح أسباب خيبة المريخ قاريًا وكشفت مصادر عالية الثقة، أنّ إدارة المريخ تعتزم استعادة نجمها، استجابة للمطالبات الجماهيرية الملحة، ونظرًا لقيمته الفنية العالية؛ إذ تعد عودته مكسبًا مضاعفًا باعتباره أفضل مدافع في البلاد، وسيشكل إضافة نوعية للفريق. كما يخدم هذا التوجه خطط إدارة الرئيس مجاهد سهل في التحضير للجمعية العمومية المقررة في مارس 2027 لانتخاب مجلس إدارة جديد، حيث ستحظى الإدارة بدعم كبير إذا نجحت في استعادة كرشوم الذي قدم سنوات مميزة مع الفريق، وأسهم بفاعلية في بلوغه دور المجموعات بدوري أبطال أفريقيا 3 نسخ متتالية. وقد أثارت هذه الرغبة قلق الغريم التقليدي الهلال الذي يستعد بقوة لمرحلة المجموعات. ومن المتوقع أن يحسم اللاعب مستقبله خلال الفترة المقبلة؛ ففي حال تمديد عقده مع ناديه الحالي، ستتلاشى آمال عودته للمريخ مستقبلًا، لا سيما مع بلوغه سن الـ35 عامًا، واقترابه من الاعتزال، أما في حال تعثر مفاوضات التجديد مع الهلال فسيمنح ذلك المريخ الضوء الأخضر لضمه. أخبار ذات صلة الهلال السوداني اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص 2 نوفمبر 2026 الهلال السوداني بعد رسائل الحزم.. مدرب الهلال يتلقى football.summary: تسبب نادي المريخ في إرباك تحضيرات نادي الهلال السوداني لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث عاد المدافع مصطفى كرشوم إلى الواجهة بعد تقديمه مستويات مميزة مع منتخب بلاده وناديه. يسعى الهلال للحفاظ على كرشوم، الذي يعتبر من أفضل اللاعبين في السودان، من خلال التفاوض لتمديد عقده قبل دخوله الفترة الحرة. في المقابل، يخطط المريخ لاستعادة نجمه السابق، استجابة لمطالب الجماهير، مما يزيد من حدة المنافسة بين الناديين. كرشوم، الذي ساهم بشكل كبير في نجاح الهلال في السنوات الأخيرة، قد يحسم مستقبله قريبًا. إذا نجح الهلال في تجديد عقده، ستتلاشى آمال المريخ في ضمه، خاصة مع اقتراب اللاعب من الاعتزال. بينما إذا تعثرت المفاوضات، قد يفتح ذلك المجال أمام المريخ لاستعادة خدماته، مما يزيد من التوتر بين الغريمين التقليديين في كرة القدم السودانية.

football.summary: في مباراة دوري أبطال أفريقيا التي جرت في 15 يناير 2027، انتهت مواجهة نواذيبو وبيترو أتلتيكو بالتعادل السلبي 0-0. هذه المباراة كانت ضمن مرحلة المجموعات للموسم 2026/2027، حيث يتنافس الفريقان في المجموعة A التي تضم أيضًا الترجي الرياضي التونسي ويلييت كلوب. حتى الآن، لم يحقق أي من الفرق الأربعة أي انتصارات أو تعادلات، مما يجعل المنافسة مشوقة في الجولات القادمة. المباراة كانت متاحة للمشاهدة المباشرة عبر منصة Winwin، حيث تم تقديم ملخصات وأهداف المباراة. كما تم تسليط الضوء على أخبار أخرى تتعلق بدوري أبطال أفريقيا، بما في ذلك القرعة والمباريات المرتقبة. يتطلع كل من نواذيبو وبيترو أتلتيكو إلى تحسين أدائهما في المباريات القادمة لتحقيق نتائج أفضل في البطولة.

football.summary: مباراة هورويا ضد الهلال السوداني، التي أقيمت في 15 يناير 2027، كانت جزءًا من مرحلة المجموعات لدوري أبطال إفريقيا 2026/2027. انتهت المباراة بالتعادل السلبي 0-0، مما يعكس أداءً متوازنًا بين الفريقين. في المجموعة A، يتصدر الترجي الرياضي التونسي، بينما لم يتمكن أي من الفرق الأخرى من تحقيق نقاط حتى الآن. يتضمن جدول المجموعة أندية مثل بيترو أتلتيكو ونواذيبو ويلييت كلوب، وكلها لم تلعب بعد. المباراة كانت متاحة للبث المباشر عبر منصة Winwin، حيث تم تقديم تغطية شاملة للأحداث. كما تم تناول بعض الأخبار ذات الصلة، مثل خسارة المريخ أمام هورويا في وقت سابق، مما أثار قلق جماهيره. تواصل الفرق الاستعداد لمبارياتها المقبلة في البطولة، حيث يسعى كل فريق لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في الجولات القادمة.

football.summary: تواجه الهلال السوداني فريق بيراميدز في مباراة ضمن دوري أبطال إفريقيا، حيث انتهت المباراة بالتعادل السلبي 0-0. أقيمت المباراة في 8 يناير 2027، وهي جزء من مرحلة المجموعات للموسم 2026/2027. يتواجد الهلال السوداني في المجموعة A، التي تضم أيضًا الترجي الرياضي التونسي وبيترو أتلتيكو ونواذيبو. على الرغم من عدم تسجيل أي أهداف، إلا أن المباراة كانت مثيرة، حيث حاول كلا الفريقين السيطرة على مجريات اللعب. الهلال السوداني يسعى لاستعادة توازنه بعد سلسلة من النتائج المتباينة في الدوري الرواندي، بينما بيراميدز يأمل في تحسين أدائه في البطولة. تتواصل المنافسات في دوري أبطال إفريقيا، حيث يتطلع كل فريق لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في المباريات القادمة لتعزيز فرصه في التأهل إلى الأدوار المتقدمة.
